# Introduction and problem framing {#sec-intro} Petra (shortening)

Speed dating compresses courtship into a single evening: each participant meets a series
of opposite-sex partners for a few minutes and privately decides, immediately afterward,
whether they'd like to see that person again. An event organizer, or in its modern form a
dating app deciding whose profile to surface to whom, controls one thing: who gets paired with
whom. A pairing only one side wants wastes the encounter as surely as one neither side wants,
since what matters is *mutual* interest. That makes this a **reciprocal recommendation**
problem: the target label, `match`, is symmetric by construction (@sec-data), so a good
ranking for participant A has to reflect what B is likely to think of A too. A standard
recommender objective, ranking items by predicted user preference, doesn't capture that by
itself; a candidate has to clear the bar from both directions.

The recommendation also has to come *before* the encounter: an organizer choosing a seating
chart, or an app choosing whose profile to show, can't use anything a participant reveals
during the date itself, since that information doesn't exist yet when the decision has to be
made. Every feature used here is therefore restricted to what's knowable at signup:
demographic and lifestyle profile, stated preferences over what matters in a partner,
self-ratings, and interests (@sec-features). This constraint drives the whole task's
difficulty: the strongest predictors of the decision are in-date impressions (@fig-leakage),
and a model that could see them wouldn't be measuring anything transferable to the
seating-chart problem it's meant to solve.

A second consequence of the same constraint is that every evaluation fold is a **cold start**.
Because each of the 551 participants attends exactly one of the 21 waves (@sec-data), holding
out a wave to test on removes those participants from the training data entirely; there is
no history of past acceptances or rejections to fall back on for anyone in the test set
(@sec-features). This rules out the reputation-style features ("how often is this person
usually accepted") that would otherwise dominate a popularity-driven task, and it means every
method compared here, including the baseline, must generalize from a participant's stated
profile alone.

Our research question is whether a personalized model that combines both sides' pre-date
profiles can rank reciprocal candidates better than a method that only knows how generally
desirable each candidate is. We compare three methods (a popularity baseline, a
clustering-based compatibility method, and a factorization machine) under one shared
leave-one-wave-out evaluation protocol (@sec-protocol), and report both whether each method
beats a chance-level ranking and whether the personalized methods beat the non-personalized
baseline (@sec-results). "Success" here means a ranking that recovers more of a participant's mutual matches inside a
short top-3 list than popularity alone can, without relying on information the
reciprocal-recommendation setting doesn't have access to.

# Data understanding {#sec-data} Alin Shorten

*Measurements below are tagged with where they can be reproduced: **EDA §n** means section n of the
exploratory notebook, **FE §n** section n of the feature-engineering notebook; both are named in the
reproducibility note that closes this section.*

## The dataset and the unit of observation

We use the Columbia speed-dating experiment of @fisman2006gender: 21 events, called *waves*, run
between 2002 and 2004. Within a wave every participant met each opposite-sex participant for a
four-minute date and then privately recorded whether they would like to see that person again. The
published file holds 8,378 rows over 195 columns and describes 551 participants (EDA §2).

One row is a **directed encounter** — participant `iid` meeting partner `pid`, recorded from `iid`'s
point of view — so every meeting appears twice, once from each side. We verified this mirror
structure rather than assuming it: for all 8,368 rows carrying a partner identifier the mirrored row
is present, the partner's own decision equals the `dec_o` field stored on our row on 100% of rows,
and `match` equals the conjunction of the two decisions on every row (EDA §3, FE §4).
The ten rows without a partner identifier were dropped, as no pairwise feature is defined for them.
Each participant appears in exactly one wave and no date crosses a wave boundary, which is what
makes the wave a clean unit for cross-validation (@sec-protocol).

| Property | Value | Property | Value |
|:-------------------------|:-----------|:--------------------------|:-----------|
| Rows × columns | 8,378 × 195 | Participants per wave | 10–44 (med. 24) |
| Participants / waves | 551 / 21 | Partners per participant | 5–22 (med. 16) |
| Directed encounters used | 8,368 | Acceptance rate (`dec`) | 42.0% |
| Mirrored rows present | 8,368 of 8,368 | Mutual match rate | 16.5% |

: The dataset at a glance; values from EDA §3–§6 and FE §4. {#tbl-data-summary}

Feedback is **implicit and binary**, and we retain both readings of it: the directional `dec`
records one person's decision and is the natural training target, while the symmetric `match`, true
only when both parties accept, is the relevance label for ranking. Matches are far rarer than
acceptances — 16.5% against 42.0% — so the positive class is small and accuracy would be a
misleading measure (EDA §5). Acceptance is also markedly gendered, and the distinction between
*giving* and *receiving* matters: men said yes on 47.4% of their dates and women on 36.5%;
averaged per person, women were accepted at a mean rate of 47.9% and men at 37.2% (EDA §5 and
§9). A model blind to the decider's gender is therefore miscalibrated for one of the two groups.

## Candidate sets, and whether the data can be evaluated

![Left: participants per wave, i.e. the 21 cross-validation folds. Right: partners met per
participant, which is exactly their candidate-set size. Both panels: EDA §4 and
§6.](figures/fig1_structure.png){#fig-structure
width=94%}

The candidate set needs no construction and no negative sampling, which is unusual for an offline
recommender evaluation: **every one of the 551 participants met every opposite-sex participant
present in their wave** (verified in FE §4). Each candidate list is therefore fully observed, its
length being the number of partners met — 5 to 22, median 16 (@fig-structure). Because the lists are
short, a cut-off at rank 10 would cover most of a list, which is why the evaluation reports metrics
at rank 3 (@sec-protocol).

Two properties of the data limit what those metrics can show. A substantial minority of users have
no relevant item: 18.0% obtained no mutual match, leaving their reciprocal rank undefined, and 5.6%
accepted nobody; with a median of two matches per user, precision at rank 3 is capped at 2/3 for
half the sample, so methods must be compared against each other rather than against a theoretical
1.0 (EDA §10). The 21 folds are also not equivalent — per-wave match rates run from 8.3% to 31.0%, a
3.7-fold spread — so a mean across folds without its standard deviation would conceal more than it
reports. Part of that spread is by design: `condtn`, an experimental manipulation (limited versus
extensive choice), is constant within each wave and therefore perfectly confounded with the split
unit, explaining $R^2 \approx 0.11$ of the between-wave variance in match rate and correlating at
$+0.88$ with candidate-set size. Fold difficulty is thus partly structural, and `condtn` cannot
serve as a ranking feature, since a wave-constant value reorders nothing within a wave (EDA §10.1).

Attention is unequally distributed, which is what makes a popularity baseline non-trivial: the
size-free Gini coefficient of the acceptance rate is 0.323, the most desirable 10% of participants
absorb 22.8% of all acceptances, and 4.0% receive none (EDA §9; see @sec-baseline). The sample is
also demographically skewed — 55.2% of participants are European/Caucasian and the smallest racial
groups hold roughly 26 people (EDA §8) — so per-group fairness metrics would rest on cells too thin
to interpret, which is why @sec-analysis uses gender exposure as the fairness axis instead.

## Data hygiene

Missingness in the columns we rely on is minor: identifiers, decisions and the match label are
essentially complete, while 59 of the 195 columns are more than half empty, almost all of them the
follow-up surveys this project does not use (EDA §7). @tbl-hygiene lists the audits that did require
a decision.

| Finding | Evidence | Decision |
|:--------------------|:-------------------------|:-----------------------|
| Values outside documented ranges | 617 cells over 25 columns (0.23%); `gaming` reaches 14 on a 1–10 scale | Clip to the documented range before scaling; unclipped, one 14 stretches a min–max scaler across the column |
| Preference block on two scales | Documentation warns of a 1–10 scale in waves 6–9; that block proves already converted to shares, since only those waves hold non-integer values and they invert exactly to 1–10 answers | No rescaling required; normalise each participant's six weights to sum to one, since per-wave totals in fact range 90–148 |
| Sparse pre-date columns | `expnum` 77% missing, `mn_sat` 63%, `tuition` 58%, `income` 49%, and not missing at random | Exclude all four rather than impute half a column into a fairness analysis; keep `exphappy` (1.5%) |

: Data-quality findings and the decisions they produced; the three rows are established in EDA
§14.1, §12 and §7.1 respectively. {#tbl-hygiene}

One residual issue cannot be repaired and is reported rather than fixed. Waves 6–9 answered a
*different question*: participants rated each attribute from 1 to 10 instead of distributing 100
points across six attributes. Normalisation equalises the scale but not the question. Conversion
discards intensity — a participant answering 9 to all six becomes indistinguishable from one
answering 2 to all six — and the rating format elicits flatter profiles: on the identical normalised
scale, waves 6–9 profiles are 2.7 times less spread out, and none of those participants gave any
attribute zero weight against 20.2% elsewhere, because a minimum answer of 1 always leaves a positive
share. This affects 101 of 541 participants and 4 of the 21 folds (EDA §12.1).

## Reproducibility

All analysis code lives in the repository rather than in this report:

- `01_Speed_Dating_EDA.ipynb` — the exploratory analysis, cited above as **EDA §n**;
- `02_Speed_Dating_Feature_Engineering.ipynb` — the feature construction, cited as **FE §n**. It
  narrates and verifies `sd_features.py`, the module holding the feature logic, so that the
  modelling and evaluation steps import one definition rather than reimplementing it;
- `03_Baseline_Desirability_Model.ipynb` — the popularity baseline of @sec-baseline
  (`baseline_desirability.py`);
- `04_X1_Clustering.ipynb` and `04_Speed_Dating_Factorization_Machine.ipynb` — the two candidate
  methods, developed in parallel and sharing the `04` prefix: the cluster-based method
  (`x1_cluster.py`, ranking metrics in `evaluation.py`) and the factorization machine of
  @sec-method (`sd_fm.py`).

All notebooks run top to bottom from a cold kernel on Python 3.11.9 with the pinned
`requirements.txt` and a fixed seed (`SEED = 42`); `make_report_figures.py` regenerates the figures
above, and the exported feature table is committed alongside a generated data dictionary giving the
definition, source, documented range and missingness of every column.

## Feature set and leakage boundary {#sec-features}

### Where the boundary lies

Since the system must recommend pairings *before* the event, a feature is admissible only if it is
known at signup. Three independent sources place the boundary identically: our own problem statement
(@sec-intro), the project proposal, and the leakage note in the dataset documentation, which names
the admissible blocks explicitly (EDA §13). @tbl-leakage gives the resulting partition.

| Admissible (known at signup) | Excluded, and why |
|:----------------------------------|:---------------------------------|
| Signup profile: age, race, field, career, goal, going-out and dating frequency, importance of shared race and religion, expected happiness | Scorecard ratings `attr, sinc, intel, fun, amb, shar`, recorded *during* the date |
| 17 interest ratings, and `int_corr`, the pair's interest correlation | `like` and `prob`: recorded at the moment of decision and closely tied to it ($r = 0.51$, $0.31$) |
| Stated preference weights and their partner-side copies `pf_o_*` | The partner's in-date ratings `attr_o … prob_o`, `like_o`, `met_o` |
| Self-ratings `attr3_1 … amb3_1`; pair-level `samerace` | `dec_o` as an input: it is the reverse direction's *label* |
| Partner attributes joined on `pid` | `_s`, `_2`, `_3` surveys, recorded after the decisions; `condtn`; the four sparse columns of @tbl-hygiene |

: The pre-date feature boundary. The exclusion list is enforced programmatically in `sd_features.py`
and the check is executed in FE §10. {#tbl-leakage}

![Absolute correlation with the decision, on one axis: the in-date scorecard against the eight
strongest pre-date pair features. The remaining pre-date features are weaker
still. Correlations from EDA §11 and §13.2, and FE §9.](figures/fig2_leakage.png){#fig-leakage
width=88%}

Obeying the constraint is expensive, and @fig-leakage states the cost plainly: the signals that
dominate the decision are exactly the inadmissible ones — `like` at $|r| = 0.51$, attractiveness at
$0.49$, fun at $0.41$ — while the strongest admissible pair feature reaches $0.067$. The pre-date
task is not a weakened version of the in-date task but a substantially harder one, and comparisons
against published figures that use in-date ratings would be misleading.

A second consequence is stronger. Because participants attend exactly one wave, holding out a wave
removes those people entirely: across all 21 folds, **zero of 551 held-out participants and zero of
their partners have any training history** (EDA §15, per fold in FE §11). Every
fold is a complete cold start. Reputation features — how often a person accepts, how often they are
accepted — are the strongest pre-date signals available ($|r| \approx 0.40$ and $0.36$ estimated
leave-one-out, EDA §13.3), yet under this protocol they collapse to a constant on every test row,
and a constant cannot reorder a ranked list. They are therefore excluded by decision rather than
oversight, and the same fact re-specifies the baseline (@sec-baseline).

### The engineered feature set

The feature table holds 8,368 directed encounters described by 95 features, the decider's gender
and six blocks (@tbl-features), plus identifiers and both labels. Partner attributes are attached
by a map-join on `pid`; we verified that the ready-made `pf_o_*` block is identical to the
partner's own stated preferences before relying on either (FE §4 and §6).

| Block | № | Example and rationale |
|:------------------|----:|:---------------------------------------------|
| Decider gender | 1 | `gender`: acceptance rates differ by gender (EDA §5) |
| Profile, both sides | 20 | `age`, `goal`, `go_out`: the demographic basis of a content model |
| Stated preferences | 12 | `pref_attr`: what each side says it wants, as shares summing to one |
| Self-ratings | 10 | `selfrate_attr`: the pre-date stand-in for what a person is like |
| Interests | 34 | `hiking`, `museums`: signup interest profiles for both sides |
| Dyadic comparisons | 12 | `age_diff`, `samerace`, `race_importance`, `int_corr` |
| Compatibility | 6 | `compat_a2b`, `compat_b2a`, `compat_harmonic` |

: The 95 engineered features, built in FE §5–§9; full definitions are in the exported data
dictionary. {#tbl-features}

The compatibility block carries the reciprocal idea. The natural formulation — the distance between
one person's stated preferences and the attribute ratings their partner received — is unavailable
here, since those ratings are in-date and, for a cold-start partner, absent from training
altogether. We substitute the partner's **self-ratings**, collected at signup and present for 98.4%
of participants across all 21 waves, and score each direction separately: `compat_a2b` applies the
decider's preference weights to the partner's self-rated attributes, `compat_b2a` is the mirror
image, and `compat_harmonic` is their harmonic mean, a single symmetric score (EDA §15.4,
built in FE §9).

![Stated preference weights against the weights implied by participants' actual decisions, by gender;
both normalised to sum to one. Source: EDA §12.](figures/fig3_stated_revealed.png){#fig-stated-revealed width=94%}

Two observations motivate the construction. Stated and revealed preferences genuinely diverge, and
diverge differently by gender (@fig-stated-revealed): both groups act on shared interests and fun
considerably more than they claim to, and on sincerity and intelligence considerably less. Were the
two aligned, a compatibility feature would add nothing beyond the attributes themselves. The two
directions also behave as correctly oriented directional features must: `compat_a2b`, which asks
whether the partner matches *the decider's* criteria, correlates $+0.067$ with the decider's own
decision, whereas its mirror `compat_b2a` does not ($-0.023$); against the symmetric `match` label
the two are equal, at $+0.037$ each (FE §9). Had the join been inverted, these signs would have
reversed. The sign pattern confirms the join's orientation; it does not show that weighting by
stated preferences adds information beyond the partner's self-ratings, which is what the model
comparison in @sec-results tests.

### Leakage discipline in preprocessing

Preprocessing separates two kinds of operation. Clipping and min–max scaling use the *documented*
ranges from the data key rather than observed extrema, so they learn nothing from the data and
cannot leak, and a value means the same thing in every fold. Everything estimated — standardisation,
median imputation — is fitted on the training waves alone and applied to the held-out wave, because
a scaler fitted on the full table has already seen the fold it will be evaluated on. Categorical
codes are one-hot encoded against fixed category lists from the documentation, so the design matrix
keeps identical width across all 21 folds even when a fold contains no instance of a category. The
exported table is consequently unscaled by design, with the transformation applied inside the
cross-validation loop (FE §12; ranges audited in EDA §14).

# Baseline {#sec-baseline}

The baseline is a **popularity ranking**: candidates are ordered by desirability, the rate at which
they are accepted, ignoring who is choosing. It is a meaningful rather than a trivial reference
precisely because attention is concentrated — a size-free Gini of 0.323, the top decile absorbing
22.8% of acceptances (EDA §9) — so a ranker that merely learns who is popular already captures a
real regularity that a personalised method must beat.

The exploratory analysis established that it cannot be computed as usually worded (EDA §15.1):
ranking by "acceptances received" presumes a history, and under leave-one-wave-out no held-out
participant has one. Of the three available resolutions, computing desirability *within* the test
wave uses the labels being predicted and is admissible only if declared as a deliberately
optimistic, transductive upper bound, while scoring all candidates identically is leakage-free but
reduces the baseline to a random shuffle. We therefore adopt **predicted desirability**: a model
trained on the training waves that predicts a participant's acceptance rate from their signup
profile alone, then applied to unseen participants. This preserves what a popularity baseline is
meant to be — global, non-personalised, independent of who is choosing — while remaining computable
for a cold start. The training-side desirability the model is fitted against is not a raw
acceptance rate but a **Wilson lower bound** on it [@wilson1927probable]: the acceptance rate we can
be confident a participant is achieving *at least*, given how many dates that estimate rests on. The
bound is deliberately pessimistic: it pulls every rate down, and pulls it further when the rate
comes from only a few dates. A participant accepted by 4 of 4 partners is scored 0.51 rather than
1.00, while one accepted by 40 of 50 is scored 0.67 rather than 0.80 — much closer to its raw
value, since 50 dates is enough evidence to largely trust it. This is what keeps a small, lucky sample from
outranking a larger, more reliable one.

Under the protocol of @sec-protocol, the baseline reaches a mean Recall@3 of 0.350 (SD
0.216) and NDCG@3 of 0.348 (SD 0.179) across the 21 folds, with Precision@3 = 0.260, MRR =
0.480, and Coverage@3 = 0.276; it recommends from roughly a quarter of the candidate pool,
consistent with a ranking that repeats the same generally-desirable participants across waves.
Tested against a randomized ranking of the same candidates (@sec-protocol), the baseline's
NDCG@3 is higher in 15 of 21 folds and the improvement is significant by both a paired
$t$-test ($p=0.011$) and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test ($p=0.016$): predicted desirability
captures a real, non-random regularity in who gets accepted, even though it uses no
information about who is doing the choosing.

Results for this baseline are reported alongside the proposed method in @sec-results, under the
shared protocol of @sec-protocol.

# Method {#sec-method}

## Clustering {#sec-clustering} Petra Shorten

Our first personalized method groups participants by profile similarity rather than modelling
the accept/reject decision directly. It exploits a gender asymmetry from the data-understanding
stage (@fig-stated-revealed): what men report *being like* and what women report *wanting* are
the more informative sides of each stated block, so men are clustered on five self-ratings
(`selfrate_attr` ... `selfrate_amb`) and women on four preference weights (`pref_attr`,
`pref_sinc`, `pref_intel`, `pref_fun`), each with $k$-means, $k=4$ per side, fit on
standardized, median-imputed inputs. Two of the six stated-preference weights, `pref_amb` and
`pref_shar`, are excluded from the clustering distance since they're exactly zero for a
substantial minority of women (12 and 14 of 274) and would otherwise let that zero inflation
dominate the split; they're retained instead as per-person zero-indicator features.

Every training pair falls into one of $4\times4=16$ (male-cluster, female-cluster) cells.
Within the training waves of each fold we build three lookup tables over these cells: the rate
at which women in a cell said yes to men in the paired cluster, the rate at which men said yes
to women in the paired cluster, and the mutual match rate. Each cell average is shrunk toward
the fold's global rate with $m=20$ pseudo-counts, the same convention used for the behavioural
features in @sec-features, so a cluster pairing seen only a handful of times in training does
not receive an extreme score. A held-out participant needs no training history to be scored: cluster assignment applies the
fold's fitted $k$-means directly to their own signup profile, satisfying the same cold-start
requirement as the other two methods (@sec-features). At
prediction time each directed encounter is scored by the table appropriate to its decider: the
female-decision table on a woman's row, the male-decision table on a man's. The ranking a woman
sees over her candidates is therefore built from other women's revealed behaviour in her own
cluster pairing.

This method is coarser than the factorization machine by design: it discards all profile
information beyond the clustering axes and represents compatibility as a $4\times4$ table
rather than a learned interaction over 95 features. Comparing it against both the baseline and
the factorization machine (@sec-results) tests whether a simple, interpretable compatibility
structure captures reciprocal preference as well as either a non-personalized ranking or a
fully learned one.


## Factorization Machine {#sec-factorization-machine}


Our improved method is a factorization machine (FM), a model that combines a
linear predictor with learned pairwise feature interactions [@rendle2010factorization]. We train it
on the directional decision `dec`: for a directed encounter $A \rightarrow B$, the target is one if
participant $A$ would like to meet participant $B$ again. The input contains the full pre-date
feature representation described in @sec-features. After fold-specific imputation, scaling and
one-hot encoding, the 95 declared features form a 181-dimensional design matrix. Participant
identifiers are used only to join the two directions of an encounter and never enter the model
this is necessary because every held-out participant is a complete cold start. 

For a feature vector $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, the FM predicts the directional logit

$$
\hat y(\mathbf{x}) = w_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{d}w_i x_i
+ \sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{j=i+1}^{d}\langle\mathbf{v}_i,\mathbf{v}_j\rangle x_i x_j,
$$

where $w_0$ is the global bias, $w_i$ are linear coefficients, and
$\mathbf{v}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ is the latent vector associated with feature $i$. The inner product $\langle\mathbf{v}_i,\mathbf{v}_j\rangle$ parameterises an interaction without
estimating a separate coefficient for every feature pair. Rather than enumerating all
$\binom{181}{2} = 16{,}290$ feature pairs, `sd_fm.py` computes the pairwise interaction term with
the exact rearrangement of @rendle2010factorization, which yields the same value at a cost of $O(dk)$ instead of $O(d^2k)$. Setting
$k=0$ removes the interaction term and yields a linear logistic model through the same code path.

The model is fitted in PyTorch by minimizing binary cross-entropy with logits plus an explicit
$L_2$ penalty on the linear and latent weights,
$\mathcal{L}=\operatorname{BCE}+\lambda(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2^2+
\lVert\mathbf{V}\rVert_F^2)$. We use full-batch Adam and a fixed random seed of 42. Early stopping on
validation log-loss (patience 20 epochs) is used only during hyperparameter selection, where it
fixes the epoch budget; the 21 outer fits then train for that fixed number of epochs. For each
outer held-out wave, the preprocessor and FM weights are refitted using only the other waves; the held-out wave is
transformed with that fold's fitted preprocessor.

Reciprocity is introduced after directional prediction. The fitted model produces
$p_{A\rightarrow B}$ and $p_{B\rightarrow A}$ from the two mirrored rows, which are combined into
the symmetric reciprocal score

$$
s(A,B)=\frac{2p_{A\rightarrow B}p_{B\rightarrow A}}
{p_{A\rightarrow B}+p_{B\rightarrow A}}.
$$

The harmonic mean assigns a high score only when both directional predictions are high and gives
the pair the same score from either participant's perspective. We use it as a ranking score rather
than interpreting it as a calibrated probability of a mutual match. The symmetric `match` label is
therefore reserved for evaluating the resulting candidate rankings and is not used to train the
directional model.

Hyperparameters were selected once using a grouped validation split for computational efficiency.
Wave 1 was excluded from tuning; from the remaining 20 waves, four seeded waves formed the inner
validation set and the rest the inner training set. The search considered
$k\in\{4,8,16\}$, $\lambda\in\{0.001,0.01,0.02,0.05\}$ and learning rates in
$\{0.01,0.05\}$. Configurations were compared by validation log-loss, while early stopping supplied
the epoch budget. The selected configuration ($k=16$, $\lambda=0.05$, learning rate $0.05$, 40
epochs) was then reused for every outer fit. Because waves used during tuning also appear in the
outer evaluation, this is a non-nested cross-validation design and its performance estimate may be
mildly optimistic.

# Evaluation {#sec-eval}


## Protocol {#sec-protocol} Alison Shorten

Evaluation follows **leave-one-wave-out cross-validation**: each of the 21 waves is held
out in turn as the test fold while the model is fit on the remaining 20, so every held-out
participant is a complete cold start (@sec-baseline, @sec-clustering, @sec-factorization-machine).
This mirrors the natural unit of the data, a closed pool of participants who only ever meet
each other, and avoids the leakage a random split would introduce by placing both sides of an
encounter, or an encounter and its wave-mates, on opposite sides of the split.

The relevance label is the mutual outcome `match == 1`: both participants said yes. This is
stricter than the directional decision `dec` used to train the factorization machine and the
clustering method's per-direction tables (@sec-method), which is deliberate: evaluation asks
whether a *reciprocal* recommendation was surfaced, not whether one side alone was interested.

The candidate set requires no construction: as established in @sec-data, every participant met
every opposite-sex participant in their wave, so each held-out participant's candidate list is
exactly the partners recorded for their wave, fully observed with no negative sampling and no
exposure bias to guard against. No additional filtering applies: the recorded pairs are already the eligible set.

Rankings are cut off at $k=3$: candidate lists run 5-22 partners (median 16, @fig-structure),
short enough that a conventional cutoff like 10 would cover most of a list and say little
about ranking quality. Two relevance metrics are reported, Recall@3 and NDCG@3, plus
Precision@3 and MRR as supporting detail, alongside one beyond-accuracy metric, Coverage@3, the share of the candidate pool that ever appears in a top-3 list, which speaks to the fairness
discussion in @sec-analysis. All three methods compared in @sec-results (the popularity baseline, the clustering method, and the factorization machine) are scored by the same
evaluator function, so tie-breaking, the relevance-population convention, and every metric
definition are held identical across methods rather than reimplemented per method.

To confirm that "beats chance" is not assumed, each method's per-fold NDCG@3 is compared
against a fully randomized ranking of the same candidates (50 random shuffles per fold,
averaged) using a paired $t$-test and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test across the 21 folds. This randomized ranking serves only as a chance-level reference, not a fourth compared method,
and addresses directly whether an observed metric gain reflects the model or noise from a
small, unevenly-sized set of folds (@sec-data notes the 21 folds are not equivalent).

## Results {#sec-results} Petronella

@tbl-results summarizes all three methods under the protocol of @sec-protocol;
@fig-results shows the same means with fold-level standard deviations, plus Coverage@3 on its
own axis.

| Method | Recall@3 | NDCG@3 | Precision@3 | MRR | Coverage@3 | vs. chance ($p$, folds won) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Popularity baseline (Z) | 0.350 (0.216) | 0.348 (0.179) | 0.260 (0.124) | 0.480 (0.143) | 0.276 (0.131) | $p=0.011$, 15/21 |
| Clustering (X1) | 0.239 (0.136) | 0.254 (0.110) | 0.210 (0.094) | 0.417 (0.101) | 0.649 (0.138) | $p=0.128$, 7/21 |
| **Factorization machine (FM)** | **0.360 (0.177)** | **0.368 (0.131)** | **0.272 (0.087)** | **0.512 (0.123)** | 0.649 (0.128) | $p<0.001$, 17/21 |

: Mean (SD) across 21 leave-one-wave-out folds. Best value per relevance column in bold. The
last column reports the paired $t$-test $p$-value against a randomized-ranking chance baseline
and the number of folds where the method beat chance. {#tbl-results}

![Ranking quality at $k=3$ (left) and candidate-pool coverage (right) across the three
methods, mean over 21 folds with standard-deviation error
bars.](figures/comparison_results.png){#fig-results width=95%}

The clustering method is the clearest failure of the three: it does not reliably beat a
chance-level ranking (7 of 21 folds, $p=0.128$), and it is the only method whose mean NDCG@3
sits *below* the popularity baseline. Collapsing each side of a pairing to one of four clusters
throws away most of the profile information the other two methods use, and the resulting
$4\times4$ compatibility table is simply too coarse to separate genuine reciprocal fits from
noise at this sample size: interpretable, but not competitive.

The factorization machine reaches the best mean value on every relevance metric and is the
only method that clears chance with high confidence ($p<0.001$ by both tests, 17 of 21 folds).
Its advantage over the popularity baseline is real in direction: higher NDCG@3 in 14 of 21
folds, mean difference $+0.020$. But the paired comparison between the two is not statistically
significant ($p=0.435$ $t$-test, $p=0.229$ Wilcoxon), and 21 folds is a small sample for that
kind of test. The between-fold variance documented in @sec-data (match rates from 8.3% to
31.0%) means a handful of unusually easy or hard waves can dominate the comparison, so this is
best read as an open question rather than a settled negative. Both personalized signals point
the same direction as the baseline's popularity signal: the interaction terms the FM learns,
and the compatibility structure the clustering method encodes far more coarsely. Only the combination of a much richer feature representation (the FM's 181-dimensional design
matrix, @sec-factorization-machine) with the same protocol produces a numerically better
ranking, though whether that holds up as significant with more waves of data stays an open
question.

Coverage@3 tells a complementary story: the baseline concentrates its top-3 slots on 27.6% of
the candidate pool (a direct consequence of ranking by a single predicted-popularity score that is largely invariant across deciders), while both personalized methods, whose scores
depend on who is asking, spread recommendations across 64.9% of candidates. A wider spread is
not automatically better (@sec-analysis returns to this from a fairness angle), but it does
show that personalization changes *which* candidates get surfaced, not only how well the
surfaced ones perform.

# Analysis and Limitations {#sec-analysis} Andrin 

## Analysis

The (@sec-results) showed that the factorization machine ranks best on every relevance metric. However, the difference between the popularity baseline and the factorization machine is small and statistically insignifant. A further finding was that there was no difference between a factorization machine with a non-linear interaction term compared to a simpler factorization machine without it. This finding suggests that nothing is gained by modelling how one participant's attributes interact with their partner's.
The clustering method fails for the simple reason that it cannot tell its candidates apart. Each participant is placed in one of four groups per gender, and a candidate's score depends only on which group they land in. A woman ranking sixteen men therefore sees at most four different scores, so most of her candidates have exactly the same score and her top three are picked largely at random. 

## Fairness: Coverage

Coverage@3 is the share of a wave's candidates who appear in anyone's top three. The popularity baseline surfaces only 27.6% of the pool, while both personalized methods reach 64.9%. This matters because attention in this data is already concentrated: the most desirable tenth of participants receive 22.8% of all acceptances and 4.0% receive none (@sec-data). A popularity ranking simply repeats that pattern, recommending the same well-liked people to everyone. The factorization machine is the better case, reaching more than twice as many candidates while still ranking best on accuracy. The clustering method reaches the same coverage for a different reason: most of its candidates score identically, so the random tie-break, not the model, decides who gets shown.

## Fairness: Exposure by gender

Both the baseline and the clustering method are essentially gender-neutral, while the factorization machine shows the largest gap: men's rankings score 0.031 higher in NDCG@3 than women's.
 @tbl-gender reports each method's NDCG@3 separately
for women and men as deciders.

| Method | Women's NDCG@3 | Men's NDCG@3 | Gap (men minus women) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Popularity baseline (Z) | 0.294 | 0.298 | +0.004 |
| Clustering (X1) | 0.250 | 0.248 | -0.002 |
| Factorization machine (FM) | 0.308 | 0.339 | +0.031 |

: NDCG@3 by decider gender, pooled across all 21 folds. {#tbl-gender}

Both the baseline and the clustering method are close to gender-neutral by this measure, unsurprising for the baseline, since predicted desirability is fit on one pooled model, and for
clustering, since its compatibility tables are already split by gender by construction. The
factorization machine, the best-performing method overall, is also the one with the largest
gender gap: men's rankings score 0.031 higher in NDCG@3 than women's, alongside the acceptance
asymmetry already reported in @sec-data (men accepted 47.4% of partners, women 36.5%).

This is not because women have fewer matches to find, since matches are symmetric and both sides have the same number. The more likely cause is the training signal: women said yes to 36.5% of their partners against men's 47.4%, so the model sees proportionally fewer examples of a woman's "yes" and learns that side less well.

## Sample and era

Beyond the gender gap, the sample itself is a limitation worth stating plainly: 551 graduate
and professional students at one university, in speed-dating events run in 2002-2004
[@fisman2006gender]. Norms around dating, and what "speed dating" even means as a format, have
shifted since; nothing here generalizes to a general-population dating app two decades later,
and every metric in @sec-results should be read as an estimate over this specific population.

# Responsible use of AI tools

We used Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant) as a working tool throughout this part of the
project, but the underlying work is ours: we extended our shared evaluator (`evaluation.py`)
with the additional metrics and significance tests, decided which methods and evaluation
choices belonged in the final comparison, and built the pipeline that runs all three methods
through that shared evaluator. We used Claude for debugging the environment, for help writing
the adapter and notebook code around that pipeline, and for assisting with drafting and editing
text for several report sections. Throughout, we directed the work through iterative prompting
rather than accepting output as-is, verified the code by confirming it ran correctly and
matched expected results, and reviewed and edited all drafted text ourselves before including
it here.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion} Alin

We built and compared three reciprocal recommenders for pre-date pairing under one shared,
leave-one-wave-out evaluation protocol: a popularity baseline, a gender-asymmetric clustering
method, and a factorization machine. The factorization machine ranks best on every relevance
metric and is the only method that reliably beats chance, but its edge over the popularity
baseline isn't statistically significant at 21 folds, and the clustering method underperforms
both. A natural next step is collecting or simulating more waves, or pooling several
speed-dating datasets under the same protocol, to test whether the factorization machine's
numerical edge over the baseline holds up as significant with more folds.
